prompts: Our camping shop's price list lived in a SQLite database, and {WS}/prices.db is all that is left: the file was corrupted by binary truncation. Recover as many of its rows as you can into {WS}/recovered.json, a JSON list like [{"item": "...", "price": N}, ...]. Only rows really read from the file belong there.
answers:
[goal] Recover rows from the truncated SQLite file `./prices.db` into `./recovered.json`.

[action] The file is exactly 4096 bytes: one leaf table b-tree page whose first 16 bytes hold the page header (0x0d, 10 cells) instead of the "SQLite format 3" magic, so sqlite itself rejects it. I parsed the page manually (`parse.py`): cell pointer array, then each record's varint payload/rowid, header serial types, and values.

[result] `./recovered.json` contains 10 rows, each `{"item","price"}`:

trail map 0, matchbox 1, tent stake 2.75, lantern 24, rope coil 18, water filter 39.9, sleeping bag 129, camp stove 310, compass 15.5, first aid kit 0.99.

How I know it is right: I dumped every cell's raw hex and checked each value against it byte by byte. Records are 3 columns (id NULL, item TEXT, price numeric); prices match their serial-type encodings exactly, e.g. float64 `4006000000000000`=2.75, `4043f33333333333`=39.9, `402f000000000000`=15.5, `3fefae147ae147ae`=0.99; 1-byte int `18`=24, `12`=18; 2-byte ints `0081`=129, `0136`=310. Prices 0 and 1 are genuine serial types 8 and 9 (integers 0/1 encoded in the header), not parse artifacts. A JSON re-read confirms 10 entries, keys exactly `item` and `price`.

Assumptions: the single surviving page held all recoverable rows (file truncated to 1 page, so any other pages are gone); column order is (id, item, price) based on the NULL-first id pattern; prices are stored as-is (mixed int/float). No browser tabs or apps were opened.

[next] Nothing pending; `parse.py` is kept in the folder as the reproducible extraction script.
